title: Philosophy
text:
Principles shaped by building decision systems that must be trusted, explainable, and durable. These are not abstract ideas—they are patterns that consistently lead to reliable outcomes in environments where decisions carry operational, financial, or clinical consequences.



Effective systems begin with a clear understanding of the decision being made, the constraints surrounding it, and the risks of getting it wrong. Data serves as an input, not the anchor. A model produces a prediction; a system produces a decision. My focus is on the latter.
Key considerations include:

The structure of the decision: Mapping how a choice is actually executed in the field.
The incentives and failure modes: Identifying what happens when the system is wrong and who bears the cost.
The operational environment: Designing for the specific latency and throughput requirements of the business.

This orientation ensures solutions align with real-world decision dynamics rather than purely statistical elegance.




Ambiguity is the enemy of reliability. Before expanding feature sets or exploring advanced architectures, the foundation must be clarified:

Defining “Good”: Establishing gold-standard labels that reflect business reality, not just available data.
Defining Failure: Explicitly documenting what constitutes a system-level error versus a tolerable model variance.
Identifying Constraints: Surfacing regulatory or technical limits before they become architectural bottlenecks.

Clear definitions early on prevent downstream reliability issues and create a stable base for technical work.




High-stakes systems must be predictable, auditable, and robust under pressure. Reliability takes precedence over novelty.
Core practices include:

Interpretability Over “Black Boxes”: Prioritizing models that stakeholders can trust and auditors can verify.
Deterministic Guardrails: Wrapping probabilistic models in deterministic rules to ensure safety at the “edges”.
Fail-Safe Design: Ensuring systems are designed to fail safely toward human expertise, not away from it.

The objective is dependable performance, not algorithmic experimentation.




Regulatory requirements, workflow bottlenecks, and human review patterns are integral components of system design. Incorporating these constraints early produces solutions that integrate cleanly into real-world environments and withstand scrutiny.




Uncertainty is quantified explicitly and used to guide safe fallback paths, escalation logic, and human-in-the-loop review. Systems built with uncertainty in mind behave predictably even when data conditions shift.




These principles translate into concrete engineering practices that support reliability in production:

Economic-Metric Alignment: Developing evaluation metrics that map directly to P&L or clinical safety outcomes.
Scenario-Based Testing: Stress-testing systems against edge cases and adversarial patterns before deployment.
Hybrid Architectures: Blending rules-based logic with machine learning to balance interpretability and precision.
Audit-First Lifecycle: Implementing versioning and “decision-tracing” to ensure every action is explainable years later.
Data Quality as a Lever: Treating data pipelines as a core reliability component, not just a plumbing task.





These principles consistently produce systems that:

Improve decision quality without increasing operational burden.
Hold up under regulatory and audit scrutiny.
Scale across teams, workflows, and product surfaces.
Build trust with stakeholders who depend on the outcomes.

title: About
text:
I’m a Principal Data Scientist specializing in high‑stakes decision systems across regulated and operationally complex domains. My work focuses on building models and workflows that organizations can trust, especially when the cost of a wrong decision is high.
I approach data science by modeling the decision, not just the dataset. That means reducing ambiguity before increasing complexity, aligning statistical rigor with operational constraints, and designing systems that are reliable, explainable, and durable in real‑world environments.
My experience spans fraud detection, clinical workflow optimization, compliance automation, and risk‑aware modeling frameworks. Across these areas, I focus on measurable impact, auditability, and the ability for systems to operate under real constraints rather than idealized assumptions.
My background blends data science, risk modeling, and technical program management. That combination helps me align stakeholders, clarify requirements, and deliver systems that work beyond the prototype stage.

title: Case Studies
text: Work delivered in environments where decisions carry real consequences. These case studies highlight systems built to perform under operational pressure, regulatory expectations, and measurable performance standards. Each project reflects a commitment to clarity, rigor, and durable impact.

title: Case Studies
text:
Fraud Detection
Fintech | High‑stakes classification | Risk & compliance


Context and constraints
The organization faced rising fraud exposure, inconsistent manual review processes, and strict regulatory expectations around fairness and explainability. Existing rules‑based systems were brittle and created operational bottlenecks.


The core decision
Determine which transactions required intervention, and what the appropriate action should be for each case.


Approach
I reframed the problem from “predict fraud” to “optimize intervention decisions.” This allowed the system to incorporate cost asymmetry, operational capacity, and regulatory constraints directly into the model. I partnered with compliance, risk, and operations to define acceptable error modes and align thresholds with throughput and auditability.


Reliability strategy
I designed the system to degrade gracefully under drift, implemented monitoring for false‑positive spikes, and built transparent decision paths to satisfy audit requirements. Guardrails handled edge cases, and fallback policies ensured safe behavior under uncertainty.


Outcome shift
Fraud losses stabilized, manual review volume dropped, and compliance gained a defensible, auditable system aligned with regulatory expectations.


What this demonstrates
The ability to design and deploy decision systems that balance risk, operational constraints, and regulatory requirements.

title: Case Studies
text:
Clinical Workflow Optimization
Healthtech | Workflow modeling | Operational efficiency


Context and constraints
Clinicians were operating under high cognitive load, fragmented workflows, and inconsistent triage decisions that created bottlenecks across the care continuum. Documentation requirements, routing ambiguity, and manual review steps reduced available time for patient care. Any system introduced into this environment needed to be safe, interpretable, and aligned with clinical judgment.


The core decision
Determine which clinical tasks should be automated, escalated, or routed differently to reduce clinician burden while maintaining safety and consistency.


Approach
I mapped the end‑to‑end clinical workflow to identify decision points that created friction, delay, or unnecessary manual intervention. Working closely with clinical leaders, I defined safe automation boundaries and clarified where human oversight was essential. The resulting system combined lightweight predictive models with deterministic rules to ensure that automation supported, rather than replaced, clinical expertise.


Reliability strategy
Because clinical environments are high‑stakes and high‑variability, I built the system around reliability and safety. This included conservative thresholds, human‑in‑the‑loop review for ambiguous cases, continuous monitoring for drift, fail‑safe routing that escalated uncertainty, and transparent decision logic to maintain clinician trust.


Outcome shift
Clinicians regained meaningful time previously lost to manual triage and documentation tasks. Routing consistency improved, bottlenecks decreased, and operational throughput increased without compromising safety or clinical judgment.


What this demonstrates
The ability to design decision systems that respect domain expertise, reduce cognitive load, and improve workflow reliability in high‑pressure clinical environments.

title: Case Studies
text:
Compliance Automation
Fintech | Rule‑based + ML hybrid | Auditability


Context and constraints
The organization faced increasing regulatory scrutiny and manual compliance processes that were slow, error‑prone, and difficult to audit. Automation needed to be precise, explainable, and aligned with legal interpretations.


The core decision
Determine which cases required compliance review and what action should be taken to satisfy regulatory requirements.


Approach
I partnered with legal, compliance, and engineering to translate regulatory language into operational decision rules. I designed a hybrid system combining deterministic logic with statistical models to handle ambiguous or borderline cases.


Reliability strategy
I built audit‑ready decision logs, implemented conservative thresholds for high‑risk categories, and created a monitoring framework that alerted compliance teams to unusual patterns or potential misclassifications. These safeguards ensured the system remained transparent, defensible, and aligned with regulatory expectations.


Outcome shift
Review cycles shortened, error rates decreased, and compliance gained a transparent, scalable system that supported consistent decision‑making across evolving regulatory requirements.


What this demonstrates
The ability to operationalize regulatory requirements into reliable, auditable decision systems.
